AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily finds that countervailable subsidies were provided to producers and exporters of ripe olives from Spain. The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to four companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stefan Smith AD/CVD Operations, Office I, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-4342.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the countervailing duty order on ripe olives from Spain.[1]
On January 21, 2026, Commerce selected Agro Sevilla Aceitunas S.Coop And. (Agro Sevilla) as the mandatory respondent in this administrative review.[2]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[3]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS)
( printed page 69536)
during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[4]
On June 15, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review by 83 days.[5]
Further, on August 27, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review by 30 days.[6]
Accordingly, the deadline for the preliminary results is now November 2, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[7]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included in the Appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
The products covered by the
Order
are ripe olives from Spain. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if the parties that requested the review withdraw their requests within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. Commerce received a timely filed withdrawal requests for Plasoliva, S.L. (Plasoliva).[8]
Because the withdrawal request was timely filed, and no other parties requested a review of this company, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), we are rescinding this review of the
Order
with respect to Plasoliva.
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a countervailing duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[9]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the countervailing duty assessment rate calculated for the POR.[10]
Therefore, for an administrative review of a company to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the countervailing duty assessment rate for the POR.[11]
On August 27, 2026, we issued a memorandum notifying parties of our intent to rescind this administrative review with respect to: (1) Alimentary Group DCoop, S.Coop. And.; (2) Aceitunera del Norte de Caceres, Soc. Coop. LTDA 2° Grado; and (3) Aceitunera del Norte de Cáceres, S.C.L.[12]
We received no comments from interested parties regarding our intention to rescind the review with respect to these companies. Accordingly, in the absence of reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to these three companies, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.[13]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions, including our reliance, in part, on facts otherwise available pursuant to sections 776(a) of the Act,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Review-Specific Rate for Non-Selected Companies Under Review
There is one company for which a review was requested and for which Commerce does not intend to rescind review and which was not selected as a mandatory respondent or found to be cross-owned with a mandatory respondent, Angel Camacho Alimentación, S.L. (Camacho). The Act does not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(e)(2) of the Act. However, Commerce's regulation at 19 CFR 351.109(g) states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by following the process set forth in 19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2), which generally parallels the process for determining the all-others rate in an investigation under section 705(c)(5) of the Act. Section 705(c)(5)(A) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.109(f) state that for companies not investigated, in general, we will determine an all-others rate by weight averaging the countervailable subsidy rates established for each of the companies individually investigated, excluding zero and

de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available.[14]

articles.title: GCC launches anti-dumping probe into paper imports from India - 24 News HD
articles.summary: GCC launches anti-dumping probe into paper imports from India  24 News HD
articles.full_text:
The General Secretariat of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) announced that the Permanent Committee on Anti-Harmful Practices in International Trade has decided to open an anti-dumping investigation into imports into GCC states of uncoated writing, printing, and graphic paper in rolls or rectangular (including square) sheets, originating in or exported from India, China, and Thailand, reported Saudi Gazette on Tuesday.
The committee’s decision follows a preliminary report by the Technical Secretariat of Anti-Harmful Practices in International Trade, which operates under the GCC General Secretariat.
The initiation notice, with full details of the product under investigation and the procedures, was published in the technical secretariat’s official bulletin, Issue No. 59, dated November 2, 2026, which is available on the GCC General Secretariat’s website.
Director General of the Technical Secretariat Mahfoudh Al-Raqadi said the measures are being taken under the GCC Common Law on Anti-Dumping, Countervailing Measures and Safeguards and its executive regulations, and the World Trade Organization’s Anti-Dumping Agreement. He added that announcing the investigation gives all interested parties the opportunity to defend their interests at every stage.

articles.title: Textile-garment industry restructures supply chains to meet rules of origin - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Textile-garment industry restructures supply chains to meet rules of origin  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – More than seven years after taking effect, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) has become an important driver of Vietnam’s exports. However, fully capitalising on its tariff preferences requires businesses, particularly those in the textile and garment industry, to address challenges related to rules of origin, supply chain restructuring and value chain reorganisation. 
In response to supply challenges, textile and garment enterprises have proactively adopted more flexible supply chain strategies. 
Tran Minh Hieu, General Director of TNG Investment and Trading JSC, said that before the CPTPP came into force, the company selected material suppliers mainly based on three criteria: cost, quality and delivery time. However, with the agreement’s “yarn-forward” rule, origin compliance has become a key factor in partner selection. 
TNG has reviewed and categorised its entire supplier network, prioritising long-term cooperation with suppliers meeting origin requirements and establishing strategic partnerships with domestic fabric manufacturers. It has additionally developed an in-house software system to manage origin-related data, and use QR codes and ERP codes for each batch of imported materials and accessories, linked to relevant documents, invoices and contracts to ensure transparency and traceability. 
According to Truong Van Cam, Vice Chairman and General Secretary of the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association (VITAS), the CPTPP, which took effect in January 2019, opened access to 12 member markets. Vietnam’s textile and garment exports to these markets rose from 6.27 billion USD in 2018 to 8.3 billion USD in 2025. 
Nevertheless, the yarn-forward rule remains a major obstacle. While domestic yarn production largely meets local demand, fabric weaving, dyeing and finishing remain significant bottlenecks. Sourcing materials from within the CPTPP bloc is also challenging as member economies are not major suppliers. 
Many Vietnamese garment manufacturers still operate under the cut-make-trim (CMT) model, relying on materials supplied or designated by customers. This limits their ability to shift towards more advanced production arrangements such as free on board (FOB) and original equipment manufacturing (OEM). 
Despite expanding market access, Vietnamese goods account for just over 1% of total imports by CPTPP members. articles.summary: U.S. Trade Deficit Narrows Slightly in September  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
The U.S. goods and services deficit came in at $105.0 billion in September, a decrease of $0.7 billion from the revised August figure of $105.7 billion, according to the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. The joint release attributes the modest narrowing to a $0.7 billion reduction in the goods deficit, which fell to $135.9 billion, alongside a decline of less than $0.1 billion in the services surplus, which stood at $30.9 billion.
September exports totaled $321.5 billion, an increase of $5.8 billion over August, while imports reached $426.6 billion, up $5.2 billion from the prior month. Within goods exports, capital goods rose $3.8 billion, including a $1.3 billion gain in computers, a $0.8 billion rise in computer accessories, and a $0.7 billion increase in civilian aircraft. Foods, feeds, and beverages grew $1.9 billion on a $1.3 billion rise in soybeans, and consumer goods added $0.8 billion, helped by a $0.7 billion increase in pharmaceutical preparations. Industrial supplies and materials fell $1.0 billion, as nonmonetary gold dropped $3.4 billion while crude oil rose $1.2 billion. Services exports increased $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion.
On the import side, goods imports rose $4.4 billion to $346.9 billion. Capital goods led the gain with an $11.6 billion increase, including $7.6 billion in computers and $5.7 billion in computer accessories, partly offset by a $1.2 billion decline in semiconductors. Consumer goods added $2.4 billion on a $2.9 billion rise in pharmaceutical preparations. Industrial supplies and materials decreased $3.7 billion, with nonmonetary gold down $2.7 billion and crude oil down $1.3 billion. Services imports increased $0.8 billion to $79.7 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit declined $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports rose $297.3 billion, or 11.6 percent, and imports rose $204.9 billion, or 6.2 percent.
The three-month moving average of the goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the period ending in September. Average exports rose $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion, and average imports rose $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion. Compared with the three months ending in September 2025, the average deficit was up $36.5 billion, average exports were up $28.9 billion, and average imports were up $65.4 billion.
On a real, 2017-dollar Census basis, the goods deficit widened $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion. Real goods exports edged up $0.2 billion, or 0.1 percent, to $152.2 billion, while real goods imports rose $3.6 billion, or 1.4 percent, to $271.6 billion.
By country, September surpluses were recorded with the Netherlands at $7.7 billion, South and Central America at $6.2 billion, the United Kingdom at $3.0 billion, Hong Kong at $2.5 billion, and Australia at $2.1 billion, among others. Deficits were logged with Mexico at $28.7 billion, Vietnam at $25.3 billion, Taiwan at $21.9 billion, China at $17.9 billion, and the European Union at $14.2 billion. The deficit with Taiwan grew $3.6 billion as exports rose $0.6 billion to $5.3 billion and imports rose $4.2 billion to $27.3 billion. The European Union deficit increased $3.2 billion as exports fell $0.6 billion to $39.0 billion and imports rose $2.6 billion to $53.2 billion. The Canada deficit shrank $2.7 billion to $4.4 billion as exports fell $0.3 billion to $29.7 billion and imports fell $3.0 billion to $34.1 billion.

AGENCY:

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
Tenaska Power Services Co. (the Applicant or TPS) has applied for renewed authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 4, 2026.
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)) and regulations thereunder (10 CFR 205.300). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7151(b) and 7172(f)) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On July 7, 2026, TPS filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada for an additional five-year term. App. at 2. TPS was granted export authorization under Order No. EA-243-D on January 7, 2022, which expires on January 11, 2027. According to the Application, TPS is a Nebraska corporation that is authorized to do business in the States of Nebraska, Alabama, Illinois, Texas, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, California, Delaware, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Washington. TPS is an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of Tenaska Energy Inc. (Tenaska), which is “an independent developer and owner of power production facilities located throughout the United States.”
Id.
at 3. TPS is a “power marketer authorized by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to make sales of electric power at wholesale in interstate commerce at market-based rates.”
Id.
at 2. In addition, TPS states that it “does not currently own or control electric generation or transmission facilities, and it does not have a power supply of its own in the United States that would cause its electricity exports to have a reliability, fuel use, or system stability impact.” Furthermore, TPS states that it will “purchase the electricity that it may export, on either a firm or an interruptible basis, from wholesale generators, electric utilities, federal power marketing agencies and affiliates through negotiated agreements that have been voluntarily executed by the selling parties after considering their own need for any such electricity.”
Id.
at 5. Thus, “TPS's proposed electricity exports will not impair or tend to impede the sufficiency of electric power supplies in the United States or the regional coordination of electric utility planning or operations.”
Id.
The Applicant also states that it will “make all necessary commercial arrangements and will obtain any and all other regulatory approvals required in order to carry out any electricity exports” and that it “agrees to abide by the export limits contained in the relevant export authorization of any transmission facilities over which TPS exports electricity to Canada.”
Id.
at 6.

www.energy.gov/oe/pending-applications.

Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On June 18, 2026, Heartland filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada for an additional five-year term. App. at 1. Heartland was originally granted export authorization under Order No. EA-492 on December 21, 2021, which expires on December 21, 2026.
According to the Application, Heartland is a Canadian corporation with its principal place of business in Alberta, Canada. Heartland is indirectly wholly-owned by TransAlta Corporation (TAC), which owns generation assets across Canada, but “have no franchised service area or native load obligation in Canada or the United States.”
Id.
at 3. TAC also indirectly holds interests in U.S. companies that own electric generation facilities in the United States. Heartland is a power marketer in the United States and is “authorized by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to market electric energy and capacity at wholesale pursuant to market-based rate authorization.”
Id.
at 3-4. In addition, Heartland states that “none of Heartland's affiliates owns any electric transmission facilities other than generator interconnection facilities and Heartland is not affiliated with an entity that holds a franchise or service territory. Thus, Heartland has no “transmission system” of its own on which power exports could have a reliability or stability impact.”
Id.
at 10-11.
Heartland expresses that it is seeking authorization to “continue its exports of electrical energy acquired from the owners of U.S. generating sources and other power marketers to Canada over international electric transmission facilities and its imports from generation sources in Canada to the United States, including resources affiliated with TAC. The Presidential Permits under which the relevant border facilities were constructed and maintained, and details related thereto, are set forth in Exhibit C.”
Id.
at 9. The Applicant also states that “in making the necessary commercial arrangements and obtaining transmission capacity necessary to export electricity under the authorization requested herein, Heartland will comply with existing industry procedures for obtaining transmission capacity, including reserving transmission service in accordance with FERC's Open-Access Same-Time Information System and scheduling delivery of the export with the appropriate Regional Transmission Organization(s) or Independent System Operator(s) and/or Balancing Authority areas.”
Id.
at 13.

Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov.
Comments concerning Heartland's Application should be clearly marked with OE Docket No. EA-492-A. Comments will be posted along with the relevant application on the program website at
www.energy.gov/oe/pending-applications.
A final decision will be made on the requested authorization after the environmental impacts have been evaluated consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969, as amended (42 U.S.C. 4321,
et seq.), the DOE NEPA regulations at 10 CFR part 1021, and the DOE's Implementing Procedures (June 2026) and after DOE evaluates whether the proposed action will have an adverse impact on the sufficiency of supply or reliability of the United States electric power supply system.

AGENCY:

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that Shanghai Yueda Nails Co., Ltd., (Shanghai Yueda) and Shanghai Yueda Nails (Chuzhou) Ltd. (Chuzhou Yueda) (collectively, Yueda Nails), an exporter of certain steel nails (nails) from the People's Republic of China (China), made sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to nine companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joshua Nixon, AD/CVD Operations, Office VIII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-8361.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2026, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on nails from China.[1]
On January 28, 2026, Commerce selected Yueda Nails as the mandatory respondent in this review.
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days,[2]
and, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and
( printed page 69542)
Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[3]
On June 4, 2026, Commerce extended the preliminary results deadline by 90 days.[4]
On September 4, 2026, Commerce extended the preliminary results deadline an additional 22 days.[5]
Accordingly, the deadline for these preliminary results is now October 30, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[6]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
7
The products covered by the scope of this
Order
are nails from China. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of an antidumping duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[8]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[9]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the calculated antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[10]
Commerce notified all interested parties of its intent to rescind the instant review regarding the companies listed in Appendix II because there were no reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, and invited interested parties to comment.[11]
No party commented on this memorandum. In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review for the companies listed in Appendix II, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Act. We calculated export prices in accordance with section 772 of the Act. Because China is a non-market economy (NME) country within the meaning of section 771(18) of the Act, we calculated normal value in accordance with section 773(c) of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Separate Rates
In the
Initiation Notice,
we informed parties that firms for which the review was initiated that wished to qualify for separate rate status must complete, as appropriate, either a separate rate application or a separate rate certification.[12]
We preliminarily determine that Yueda Nails is eligible for a separate rate in this review. For further discussion,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
The China-Wide Entity
Commerce's policy regarding conditional review of the China-wide entity applies to this administrative review.[13]
Under this policy, the China-wide entity will not be under review unless a party specifically requests, or Commerce self-initiates, a review of the entity. Because no party requested a review of the China-wide entity, the entity is not under review, and the entity's rate (

articles.title: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
articles.summary: CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager CaremarkCVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business in...
articles.full_text:
CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.
In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.
A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.
The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year.
A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.
The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week: “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.”
He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions.
At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown.
Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.”
David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business.
 
“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement.
That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”.
The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation.
CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

Background
This preliminary determination is made in accordance with section 733(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Commerce published the notice of initiation of this investigation on April 28, 2026.[1]
On August 28, 2026, Commerce postponed the preliminary determination of this investigation and the revised deadline is now October 29, 2026.[2]

The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.

The product covered by this investigation is OCTG from the UAE. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,

This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice; nominations for shark stock assessment advisory panel.
SUMMARY:
NMFS solicits nominations for the Atlantic Highly Migratory
( printed page 69550)
Species (HMS) SouthEast Data, Assessment, and Review (SEDAR) Workshops Advisory Panel, also known as the “SEDAR Pool.” The SEDAR Pool is comprised of a group of individuals who, if selected, review data and advise NMFS on the scientific information, data, and models used in stock assessments for oceanic sharks in the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of America and Caribbean Sea. NMFS is seeking nominations for a 5-year term beginning in 2027. NMFS will consider individuals with definable interests in recreational and commercial fishing and related industries, including those from the environmental community, academia, and non-governmental organizations, for membership on the SEDAR Pool.
DATES:
Submit nominations on or before December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit nominations and request the SEDAR Pool Statement of Organization, Practices, and Procedures electronically via email to
SEDAR.pool@noaa.gov.
Karyl Brewster-Geisz or Delisse Ortiz at 301-427-8503.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
HMS fisheries (swordfish, sharks, tunas, and billfish) are managed under the 2006 Consolidated HMS Fishery Management Plan (FMP) and its amendments pursuant to the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act; 16 U.S.C. 1801et seq.) and consistent with the Atlantic Tunas Convention Act (16 U.S.C. 971et seq.). HMS implementing regulations are at 50 CFR part 635.
Background
NMFS established the SEDAR Pool consistent with section 302(g) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. NMFS may select individuals of the SEDAR Pool to review and advise NMFS on the scientific information, data, and models used in stock assessments for oceanic sharks in the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of America and Caribbean Sea. While NMFS created the SEDAR Pool specifically for consultation on Atlantic shark stock assessments, NMFS may expand consultation to other HMS, as needed.
NMFS may select individuals in the SEDAR Pool to participate in the various data and assessment workshops during the stock assessment process. The primary responsibility of selected individuals is to review and provide advice regarding the scientific information, data, and models that NMFS will use or consider for use in the relevant stock assessment. To ensure that the peer review is unbiased, individuals who participated in a data and/or assessment workshop for a particular stock assessment cannot serve as a peer reviewer for the same stock assessment. However, these individuals may be asked to attend the review workshop to answer specific questions from the reviewers concerning the data and/or assessment workshops. Members of the SEDAR Pool may serve as members of other advisory panels or committees established under section 302(g) concurrent with, or following, their service on the SEDAR Pool.
Procedures and Guidelines
A. Participants
The SEDAR Pool is comprised of individuals that represent the commercial and recreational fishing communities for Atlantic sharks, the environmental community active in the conservation and management of Atlantic sharks, and the academic community that have relevant expertise with sharks and/or stock assessment methodologies for marine fish species. Additionally, individuals who may not necessarily work directly with sharks, but who are involved in fisheries with similar life history, biology, and fishery issues may be part of the SEDAR Pool. Members of the SEDAR Pool must have demonstrated experience in the fisheries, related industries, research, teaching, writing, conservation, or management of marine organisms. The distribution of representation among the interested parties is not defined or limited.
Additional members of the SEDAR Pool may also include representatives from the 5 Atlantic Regional Fishery Management Councils, the 18 Atlantic states, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, and the relevant interstate commissions (Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission and Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commission).
If NMFS requires additional members to ensure a diverse pool of individuals for data or assessment workshops, NMFS may request individuals to become members of the SEDAR Pool outside of the annual nomination period.
SEDAR Pool members serve at the discretion of the Secretary. Not all members will attend each SEDAR workshop. Rather, NMFS will invite certain members to participate at specific stock assessment workshops dependent on their ability to participate, discuss, and offer scientific input and advice regarding the species being assessed.
NMFS is not obligated to fulfill any requests (
e.g., requests for an assessment of a certain species) that may be made by the SEDAR Pool or its individual members. Members of the SEDAR Pool who are invited to attend stock assessment workshops will not be compensated for their services, but may be reimbursed for their travel-related expenses to attend such workshops.
B. Nomination Procedures for Appointments to the SEDAR Pool
Member tenure is 5 years. Nominations are sought for terms beginning early in 2027 and expiring at the end of 2031. Nomination packages should include:
1. The name, address, phone number, and email of the applicant or nominee;
2. A description of the applicant's or nominee's interest in Atlantic shark stock assessments or the Atlantic shark fishery;
3. A statement of the applicant's or nominee's background and/or qualifications; and
4. A written commitment that the applicant or nominee shall participate actively and in good faith in the tasks of the SEDAR Pool, as requested.
C. Meeting Schedule
Individual members of the SEDAR Pool meet to participate in stock assessments at the discretion of the Office of Sustainable Fisheries, NMFS. Stock assessment timing, frequency, and relevant species will vary depending on the needs determined by NMFS and SEDAR staff. In 2027, NMFS plans to finalize the sandbar shark stock assessment and begin the bull shark stock assessment. All meetings are open for observation by the public.
Dated: November 2, 2026.
Kelly Denit,
Director, Office of Sustainable Fisheries,
National Marine Fisheries Service.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) orders on utility scale wind towers (wind towers) from India, Malaysia, and Spain would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Reviews” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Samuel Evans, AD/CVD Operations, Office IX, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-2420.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 16, 2021 (for Spain), and December 6, 2021 (for India and Malaysia), Commerce published the
Orders
in the
Federal Register
.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce published the notice of initiation of these first sunset reviews of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).[2]
On July 17, 2026, Commerce received timely and complete notices of intent to participate in the sunset reviews for the domestic interested party within the deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The domestic interested party claimed interested party status within the meaning of sections 771(9)(C) and 771(9)(F) of the Act as a U.S. manufacturer and producer of the domestic like product and as an association the majority of whose members produce the domestic like product.[4]
On July 31, 2026, Commerce notified the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that it had received notices of intent to participate from the domestic interested party.[5]
On August 3, 2026, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i), the domestic interested party filed timely and adequate substantive responses.[6]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from any respondent interested party. On August 24, 2026, Commerce notified the ITC that it did not receive a substantive response from any respondent interested parties.[7]
As a result, pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(C)(2), Commerce is conducting expedited (120-day) sunset reviews of the
Orders.
Scope of the Orders
The products covered by these
Orders
are wind towers from India, Malaysia, and Spain. For the full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Issues and Decisions Memorandum.[8]
( printed page 69547)
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in these sunset reviews, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping in the event of revocation of the
Orders
and the magnitude of the margins likely to prevail if the
Orders
were to be revoked, is provided in the accompanying Issues and Decision Memorandum.[9]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached in the Appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be directly accessed at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Final Results of Sunset Reviews
Pursuant to sections 751(c)(1), 752(c)(1) and (3) of the Act, Commerce determines that revocation of the
Orders
would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, and that the magnitude of the dumping margins likely to prevail would be weighted-average dumping margins up to 54.03 percent for India, 3.20 percent for Malaysia, and 73.00 percent for Spain.
This notice also serves as the only reminder to parties subject to administrative protective order (APO) of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305. Timely notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective, orders is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
We are issuing and publishing these final results in accordance with sections 751(c), 752(c), and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.218 and 19 CFR 351.221(c)(5)(ii).
Dated: October 30, 2026.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that Hangzhou Ailong Metal Products Co., Ltd. (Ailong) failed to establish its eligibility for a separate rate and, therefore, is part of the China-wide entity. The period of review (POR) is August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to 39 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.

Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty
Order
on light-walled rectangular pipe and tube (LWR pipe) from the People's Republic of China (China), including Ailong.[1]
On December 17, 2025, we released U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) information for comment.[2]
We received no comments on the CBP Data Release. On June 16, 2026, we issued an intent to rescind, in part, memorandum.[3]
We received no comments on Intent to Rescind, in Part.
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[4]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[5]
On June 24, 2026, we extended the preliminary results of this review to no later than November 2, 2026.[6]
Scope of the Order
The merchandise subject to this
Order
is certain welded carbon quality light-walled steel pipe and tube, of rectangular (including square) cross section, having a wall thickness of less than 4 mm.
The term carbon-quality steel includes both carbon steel and alloy steel which contains only small amounts of alloying elements. Specifically, the term carbon-quality includes products in which none of the elements listed below exceeds the quantity by weight respectively indicated: 1.80 percent of manganese, or

Order
is currently classified under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) subheadings 7306.61.50.00 and 7306.61.70.60. While HTSUS subheadings are provided for convenience and CBP's customs purposes, our written description of the scope of the

I. Introduction
Section 15E(t) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”) requires that each nationally recognized statistical rating organization (“NRSRO”) implement certain corporate governance measures.[1]
Specifically, Section 15E(t)(1) requires each NRSRO to have a board of directors, and Section 15E(t)(3) sets forth specified, mandatory duties of such board of directors.[2]
Section 15E(t)(2)(A) provides that at least half of the board of directors, but not fewer than two members thereof, shall be independent of the NRSRO, and that a portion of the independent directors shall include users of ratings from an NRSRO.[3]
Section 15E(t)(2)(C) provides that the compensation of the independent members of the board of directors of the NRSRO shall not be linked to the business performance of the NRSRO, and shall be arranged so as to ensure the independence of their judgment. Such section also provides that the term of office of the independent directors shall be for a pre-agreed fixed period, not to exceed five years, and shall not be renewable.
Section 36 of the Exchange Act authorizes the Commission, by rule, regulation, or order, to exempt, either conditionally or unconditionally, any person, security, or transaction, or any class or classes of persons, securities, or
( printed page 69615)
transactions, from any provision of the Exchange Act or any rule or regulation thereunder, to the extent that such exemption is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, and is consistent with the protection of investors.[4]
II. Exemption Request of Japan Credit Rating Agency, Ltd.
Japan Credit Rating Agency, Ltd. (“JCR”)
is
a credit rating agency registered with the Commission as an NRSRO under Section 15E of the Exchange Act for the classes of credit ratings described in clauses (i) through (iii) and clause (v) of Section 3(a)(62)(A) of the Exchange Act.[5]
On August 20, 2015, the Commission granted JCR a three-year, conditional exemption, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee.[6]
On August 17, 2018, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, the Commission granted JCR a subsequent three-year conditional exemption, that renewed for an additional two years in accordance with its terms, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee.[7]
On September 28, 2023, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, the Commission granted JCR another temporary, conditional exemption allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee through October 30, 2026.[8]
JCR has requested a continuation of such exemption that is not time-limited on the basis that Japanese law applicable to credit ratings agencies registered in Japan, including JCR, imposes requirements for strong independent oversight of credit rating agencies on the supervisory committee, a body separate from the board of directors.
Specifically, JCR has represented to the Commission that Japanese law requires (1) all Japanese credit rating agencies to adopt certain control systems for ensuring the “fair and appropriate performance” of their credit rating business, including establishment of a “supervisory committee” as a Japanese credit rating agency's internal oversight body and (2) at least one-third of the supervisory committee members (or at least two where there are three or fewer members) to be “independent members” of the supervisory committee, and prohibits the directors of the Japanese credit rating agency from serving as independent members.[9]
JCR also represented to the Commission that it has established processes to ensure compliance with the conditions in the 2023 order and that its supervisory committee fulfills the functional equivalent of the requirements applicable to an NRSRO's board of directors under Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3). For example, JCR represented to the Commission that: (1) two of the four supervisory committee members are independent members and one of the independent members is a user of ratings; (2) the supervisory committee independent members receive no prohibited compensatory fees, are not associated with JCR or any of its affiliated companies, and are disqualified from deliberation involving a rating where the member has a financial interest in the outcome of the rating; and (3) the supervisory committee independent members receive no prohibited compensation and have no more than a five-year term of office.
III. Discussion
Section 15E(p) of the Exchange Act, as added by Section 932(a)(8) of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act,[10]
requires Commission staff to conduct an examination of each NRSRO at least annually. Commission staff has examined JCR's satisfaction of the conditions in the prior orders as part of each annual examination conducted since 2016 and has determined that JCR currently satisfies the conditions in the 2023 order.
Accordingly, the Commission finds, based on such determination and on JCR's representations referred to in Section II above, that it is appropriate in the public interest and is consistent with the protection of investors to grant JCR a conditional exemption, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Section 15E(t)(2) and Section 15E(t)(3) through the supervisory committee, subject to the conditions specified below. In addition, Commission staff will continue to examine JCR's satisfaction of the conditions to this order set forth in Section IV below. If the conditions are not being fulfilled to the staff's satisfaction, the staff will consider whether to make recommendations to the Commission, as appropriate.[11]
IV. Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission finds that it is appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors to grant JCR a conditional exemption allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Section 15E(t)(2) and Section 15E(t)(3) of the Exchange Act through the supervisory committee.

Abstract:
USGS collects this information under the authority of 43 U.S.C. 3101-3104 (National Landslide Preparedness Act), which supports the mission of the USGS Landslide Hazards Program to reduce loss of life and property from landslides and improve public safety and community resilience. Under this authority, the USGS provides competitive grants to State, territorial, local, and Tribal governments to research, map, assess, and collect data on landslide hazards within their jurisdictions.
In response to USGS program announcements, applicants submit proposals describing proposed work in one or more priority areas: (a) advancing landslide hazard mapping and assessments, (b) improving landslide hazard planning and coordination, and (c) improving the dissemination and effectiveness of landslide hazard information to mitigate losses. Proposals include a project narrative, a detailed budget, resumes or curricula vitae of key staff, and applicant organization information (organization name, address, and authorized representative).
The USGS collects this information to evaluate and select proposals for funding that best meet the priorities of the Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Grant Program. Award recipients must also submit final technical reports summarizing project outcomes and, for awards spanning more than two years, annual progress reports describing work completed to date. The USGS uses these reports to monitor grantee progress and performance and to ensure accountability for federal funds. Final technical reports are made publicly available at
https://www.usgs.gov/programs/landslide-hazards/science/external-grants-overview.

AGENCY:
Agricultural Marketing Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Referendum order; amendment to referendum order.
SUMMARY:
This document extends the voting period for the referendum being conducted among eligible Florida citrus producers to determine whether they favor continuance of the marketing order regulating the handling of oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, and pummelos produced in Florida. The voting period was originally set to close November 9, 2026, and is now being extended through December 1, 2026.
DATES:
The voting period for the referendum will be extended from November 9 through December 1, 2026. Only current Florida citrus producers within the production area that produced oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, or pummelos for the fresh market during the period of August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, are eligible to vote in this referendum. Ballots delivered to AMS via U.S. mail or electronic ballot must show proof of delivery by no later than 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 1, 2026, to be included in the vote tabulation.
ADDRESSES:
Copies of the marketing order may be obtained from the office of the referendum agents at the Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1124 1st Street South, Winter Haven, FL 33880; telephone: (863) 324-3375; or from the Docket Clerk, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, STOP 0237, Washington, DC 20250-0237; telephone (202) 720-8085; or on the internet:
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-905.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Rebecca Geller, Marketing Specialist, or Christian D. Nissen, Branch Chief, Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1124 1st Street South, Winter Haven, FL 33880; telephone: (863) 324-3375; or email:
Rebecca.Geller@usda.gov
or
Christian.Nissen@usda.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Pursuant to Marketing Order No. 905, as amended (7 CFR part 905; the Order), and the applicable provisions of the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as amended (7 U.S.C. 601-674) (the Act), it is hereby directed that a referendum be conducted to ascertain whether continuance of the Order is favored by fresh citrus producers. The referendum voting period started October 19 and will run through December 1, 2026, among Florida fresh citrus producers in the Order's production area. Only current Florida citrus producers engaged in the production of oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, or pummelos for the fresh market during the period of August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, may participate in the continuance referendum.
A referendum order was published in the
Federal Register
on September 18, 2026 (91 FR 59101). The referendum order specified that the voting period would be from October 19 through November 9, 2026. USDA has received requests from industry organizations to extend the voting period for the referendum, citing the significant production, recovery, and business challenges currently facing Florida citrus producers and the need for additional time to ensure informed participation in the referendum process. To facilitate full producer participation in the referendum, USDA is extending the voting period from November 9 through December 1, 2026. During this time, USDA will continue to mail ballots to eligible voters who request a ballot. All ballots received from October 19 through December 1, 2026, will be accepted. Voters who have already submitted a ballot do not need to take further action.
USDA has determined that continuance referenda are an effective means for determining whether producers favor the continuation of marketing order programs. In accordance with § 905.83(c), USDA must conduct a referendum every six years. USDA would consider termination of the Order if less than two-thirds of the producers voting in the referendum, and less than two-thirds of the citrus volume represented in the referendum, vote in favor of continuance. In evaluating the merits of continuance versus termination, USDA will not exclusively consider the results of the continuance referendum. USDA will also consider all other relevant information concerning the operation of the Order and relative benefits and costs to producers, handlers, and consumers to determine whether continued operation of the Order would tend to effectuate the declared policy of the Act.
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. chapter 35), the ballot materials used in the referendum have been approved by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and have been assigned OMB No. 0581-0189, Fruit Crops. It has been estimated it will take an average of 20 minutes for each of the approximately 200 citrus producers to cast a ballot. Participation is voluntary. Ballots delivered to AMS via U.S. mail or electronic ballot must show proof of delivery by no later than 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 1, 2026, to be included in the vote tabulation.
Delaney Fuhrmeister, Rebecca Geller, Steven Kauffman, Christian Nissen, and Jennie Varela of the Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, are hereby designated as the referendum agents of the Secretary of Agriculture to conduct this referendum. The procedure applicable to the referendum shall be the “Procedure for the Conduct of Referenda in Connection with Marketing Orders for Fruits, Vegetables, and Nuts Pursuant to the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as Amended” (7 CFR part 900.400et seq.).
Ballots and voting instructions will be sent by U.S. mail or through electronic mail to all Florida citrus producers of record and may also be obtained from the referendum agents or their appointees.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
General notice.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will conduct a test regarding the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), a new case management system that is designed to provide a secure centralized location and standardized method for information capture, that may replace the submission of technical assistance requests by telephone or by email. This voluntary test will permit CBP to examine whether the CRTAP meets its intended use and function. This notice
( printed page 69567)
describes the test, invites trade members to participate, and sets forth participation criteria.
DATES:
The CRTAP test will commence on December 4, 2026 and will continue for a period of 45 days, subject to any extension, modification, or termination as announced in the
Federal Register
. CBP will begin to accept requests to participate in the test on November 4, 2026, and CBP will continue to accept such requests until the CRTAP test concludes. Public comments on the test are invited and may be submitted to the address set forth below until the test commences.
ADDRESSES:
Comments and questions concerning this notice or any aspect of the test, including requests to participate in the CRTAP test, may be submitted via email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cpb.dhs.gov,
with the subject line reading “Comments/Questions on CRTAP Test.”
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mary Ann Morris, Client Services Division, Trade Transformation Office, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, by email at
mary.ann.morris@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Current Trade/Client Representative Case Management System
CBP's Client Services Representatives are located in the Office of Trade (OT), Trade Transformation Office (TTO), Client Services Division (CSD). CSD seeks to improve the stakeholder (trade user) experience through supporting the trade community's use of the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) for processing cargo transactions, while also protecting the privacy of trade data. CSD operates and supports trade interaction within CBP electronic cargo processing systems by providing expertise for complex CBP trade processing problems. CSD oversees direct trade access into CBP's automated system and ensures the privacy of trade data. CSD is comprised of the following branches: (1) the Post Summary Processing Branch, (2) the Cargo Release and Partner Government Agency (PGA) Branch, (3) the Air and Truck Manifest Branch, (4) the Entry Summary and Post Summary Corrections (PSC) Branch, (5) the Automated Export System (AES) and Free Trade Zone (FTZ) Branch, and (6) the Ocean and Rail Manifest Branch.
Under the existing process, trade members contact their assigned CBP Client Representative by telephone or by email, requesting assistance in resolving technical issues the trade member may encounter and that the member is unable to resolve in-house. The Client Representative responds to trade inquiries and assists with resolving the issues. There is no centralized repository for the intake of this type of trade outreach and no feasible means of tracking the resolution of such matters.
II. General Description of the CRTAP Test
As part of its ongoing effort to modernize its client services trade interactions processes, CBP developed a case management system, entitled the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), to streamline operations by automating manual tasks and creating workflows, improve communication and collaboration throughout CSD and with the trade community, provide data analysis and measure the effectiveness of assistance provided to the trade community, and standardize the intake process for submission and resolution of technical issues.
The CRTAP test is a voluntary test that is limited to brokers, self-filers, software providers, Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) Operators, Automated Export System (AES) users, and/or Automated Manifest Systems (AMS) users. CBP will select participants based on the eligibility criteria discussed in Section IV below. The selected participants will provide their requests for technical assistance to their CBP Client Representative through a designated web address linking them to the CRTAP. CBP Client Representatives will respond to the test participants through the CRTAP, requesting additional information, as needed, and ultimately resolving the technical issues. Once an issue is resolved, the CBP Client Representative will close out the transaction using the CRTAP. At the conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will examine any feedback received, assess the feasibility of the CRTAP, and determine whether expanded use of the portal is warranted.
The CRTAP test will commence 30 days from the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. It will continue for 45-days, unless the test is extended, modified, or discontinued in a subsequent notice published in the
Federal Register
.
CBP will continuously monitor the CRTAP, examining transactions from submission to resolution, to determine whether modifications need to be made to the test while it is ongoing. Upon conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will determine whether the test needs to be expanded to additional users, whether the CRTAP meets the needs of CBP and the trade, and whether the CRTAP should become a permanent case management system.

I. Introduction
A. Background
On December 13, 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) adopted amendments to Rule 17a9(a) and (e)(18)(iv)(A) and (B) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”).[1]
Under these amendments, covered clearing agencies that provide central counterparty services for U.S. Treasury securities (“U.S. Treasury securities CCAs”) must establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to establish objective, risk-based, and publicly disclosed criteria for participation which require that any direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA submit for clearance and settlement all of the eligible secondary market transactions to which such direct participant is a counterparty, and identify and monitor the U.S. Treasury securities CCA's direct participants' submission of transactions for clearing as required under the amendments (together, the “Trade Submission Requirement”).[2]
The amendments defined what constitutes an “eligible secondary market transaction” to include, among other things, a secondary market transaction in U.S. Treasury securities of a type accepted for clearing by a registered covered clearing agency that is a repurchase or reverse repurchase agreement collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities (“repo transactions”), in which one of the counterparties is a direct participant of a covered clearing agency.[3]
The amendments also included an exclusion from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction for any repo transactions entered into between a direct participant and an affiliated counterparty (the “Inter-Affiliate Exclusion”), provided that the affiliated counterparty submit for clearance and settlement all other repo transactions to which the affiliate is a party (the “outward facing condition”).[4]
The amendments define “affiliated counterparty” as any counterparty which meets the following criteria: (i) the counterparty is either a bank (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(6)), broker (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(4)), dealer (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(5)), or futures commission merchant (as defined in 7 U.S.C. 1a(28)), or any entity regulated as a bank, broker, dealer, or futures commission merchant in its home jurisdiction; (ii) the counterparty holds, directly or indirectly, a majority ownership interest in the direct participant, or the direct participant, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in the counterparty, or a third party, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in both the direct participant and the counterparty; and (iii) the counterparty, direct participant, or third party referenced in paragraph (ii) of this definition as holding the majority ownership interest would be required to report its financial statements on a consolidated basis under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles or International Financial Reporting Standards, and such consolidated financial statements include the financial results of the majority-owned party or of both majority-owned parties.[5]
B. IIB's and SIFMA's Requests for Exemptive Relief
The Commission has received requests for exemptive relief related to transactions by non-U.S. persons and related to the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion.
On February 27, 2026, the Institute of International Bankers (“IIB”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief from the Trade Submission Requirement for certain non-U.S. transactions, specifically, the transactions of foreign financial institutions who are direct participants of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA when transacting with non-U.S. clients.[6]
IIB explained that exemptive relief was appropriate because of legal uncertainty in certain foreign jurisdictions regarding the enforceability of fundamental clearing requirements, potential registration requirements for clearing firms operating in those jurisdictions, and practical concerns about repo transactions occurring when no U.S. Treasury securities CCA is operating.[7]
On March 6, 2026, the Commission published the notice and encouraged interested persons to comment on the request for exemptive relief pursuant to Section 36 of the Exchange Act.[8]
The initial comment period for the IIB Notice closed on April 10, 2026, and the Commission then reopened the comment period, which then closed on May 29, 2026.[9]
On April 10, 2026, the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (“SIFMA”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief in two areas related to the Trade Submission Requirement.[10]

Partnerships between the U.S. Government and the state, local tribal and private sector at times necessitate the sharing of classified information. The State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector (SLTPS) Clearance Request Form facilitates this sharing by sponsoring security clearances for certain members of each sector based on either their membership on a Sector Coordinating Council (SCC)/association or their infrastructure protection job-related duties and their need-to-know. The SLTPS is designed to sponsor security clearances for state, local, tribal and private sector officials involved in the infrastructure protection mission. These partners are subject matter experts within specific industries and have specialized knowledge not available within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other Federal Departments or Agencies. Private citizens do not receive monetary compensation for their time. CISA created this program to sponsor clearances for these individuals who are not employed by or contracted with another Federal agency (the traditional means of obtaining a clearance) and must have clearances.
CISA collects necessary information through 1670-0013 to facilitate security clearances needed for sharing classified information with the vetted SLTPS Stakeholders.
The U.S. Government is authorized to ask for this information under Sections 201 and 229 of the Homeland Security Act (Pub. L. 107-296, 6 U.S.C. 121, 150), and Executive Orders 12968, 13526, 13549, 13636, and 13691 which authorize the collection of this information.
In order to begin this process of adjudicating a nominee to participate in the clearance program, federal nominators will complete the DHS Form 9014, State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector Clearance Request Form. The federal nominator will sign the form and have it approved by a senior-level official from the corresponding Federal Department or Agency. The signatures indicate the nominator and senior-level official have deemed the applicant has a CISA mission and meets the requirements and criteria as outlined in Executive Order (E.O.) 13549, the Department of Homeland Security, Classified National Security Information Program for SLTPS Implementing Directive and E.O. 13691, Sec. 4(c), and 32 CFR, Part 117, Sec. 117.22 of the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM). I. Introduction
On September 10, 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (the “Board” or the “PCAOB”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”), pursuant to section 107(b) [1]
of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (“SOX”) and section 19(b) [2]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Exchange Act”), a proposal to adopt (1) amendments to certain provisions of Quality Control (“QC”) 1000,
A Firm's System of Quality Control
(“QC 1000”); (2) related amendments to PCAOB Rule 2203A and PCAOB forms; and (3) technical amendments to Auditing Standard (“AS”) 2101,
Audit Planning
(each, an “Amendment” and collectively, the “Amendments”).[3]
The Amendments were approved by the PCAOB on September 9, 2026.[4]
On September 11, 2026, the Board adopted a technical correction to one of the proposed rules included in the Amendments and then filed the technical correction with the SEC on September 14, 2026.
The Amendments were published for comment in the
Federal Register
on September 18, 2026.[5]
We received ten comment letters from the public regarding the Amendments.[6]
This Order approves the Amendments, which we find to be consistent with the requirements of Title I of SOX and the rules and regulations issued thereunder and necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors.[7]
The Amendments and the findings with respect thereto are discussed in further detail below.
II. Background and Description of the Amendments
On September 9, 2024, the Commission approved QC 1000, an integrated, risk-based QC standard intended to replace the interim QC standards that the PCAOB had adopted in 2003.[8]
The PCAOB stated it believed QC 1000 would lead registered public accounting firms (“firms”) to significantly improve their QC systems.[9]
QC 1000 was set to become effective on December 15, 2025; however, the PCAOB subsequently delayed the effective date of QC 1000 for one year—until December 15, 2026—after considering information it received from various sources that some firms had encountered implementation challenges that, as a practical matter, may be insurmountable by the effective date.[10]
On September 9, 2026, the Board adopted the Amendments.[11]
The Amendments were preceded by a June 2026 supplemental request for comment [12]
and other outreach engaged in by the PCAOB. The Amendments were targeted to modify only certain provisions of QC 1000, as described in more detail below. Except for the targeted Amendments, QC 1000 would remain unchanged.
In the Notice of Filing of Proposed Rules, the PCAOB stated that it was proposing Amendments to QC 1000 that it believes address concerns regarding the implementation challenges identified by firms and to better align certain provisions with other quality management standards, both internationally and in the United States.[13]
As described by the Board, these Amendments are designed to reduce compliance costs while maintaining the investor protection benefits of QC 1000.[14]
According to the Board, although several of the Amendments the Board adopted better align QC 1000 with other quality management standards with which most firms are already complying,[15]
differences remain in areas where the Board continues to believe that alternative or incremental provisions of QC 1000 better address the United States' legal and regulatory environment, the needs and priorities of the Board's stakeholders, and the Board's statutory mandate of protecting investors and the public interest.[16]
( printed page 69621)
The Amendments consider the feedback the PCAOB received on its Supplemental Request for Comment and information obtained through the PCAOB's implementation support efforts (
e.g.,
workshops, stakeholder outreach, and feedback received from firms and other stakeholders regarding implementation, including implementation guidance provided by the PCAOB), among other sources.[17]
The principal Amendments adopted by the PCAOB are intended to:
Rescind the “design-only” requirement so that QC 1000 imposes requirements only on firms that are required to comply with applicable professional and legal requirements with respect to any “engagement” as defined in QC 1000 (QC 1000.06 and .07d);
Provide increased flexibility in filling certain specified roles in the QC system by permitting those roles to be assigned to non-firm personnel and divided among multiple individuals (QC 1000.12);
Rescind the requirement to have an External QC Function (“EQCF”) (QC 1000.28);
Narrow and simplify communication requirements relating to metrics that the firm communicates to external parties about its audit practice, firm personnel, or engagements (QC 1000.53e);
With respect to identified engagement deficiencies, require evaluation of whether similar engagement deficiencies exist on other engagements only if the identified deficiency resulted or could result in (i) a failure to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to support the conclusion reached on an engagement or (ii) an inappropriate overall conclusion on the subject matter of an engagement (QC 1000.68d);
Revise the definition of QC deficiency to make clear that, when firms have implemented more than one quality response to address the same quality risk, they can take those other quality responses (e.g.,
compensating responses) into account when determining whether a QC deficiency exists (QC 1000.A8);
Allow firms to select the date as of which they annually evaluate the effectiveness of their QC system, rather than requiring firms to evaluate as of September 30 (QC 1000.77);
Revise the QC system evaluation conclusions to align more closely with the conclusions in other quality management standards,[18]
while retaining a structured process, including specified factors for consideration, to guide the evaluation (QC 1000.77 and .78); and
Simplify the requirements for retention of QC system documentation and abbreviate the retention period from seven to five years (QC 1000.84 and .86).[19]
The Amendments will be effective on December 15, 2026, the same effective date as the rest of QC 1000.[20]
