AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule adopting as final the revisions to the capital adequacy rule and the member business lending rule made under an interim final rule (IFR) published in the
Federal Register
on April 27, 2020.
DATES:
The final rule is effective on November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John H. Brolin, Senior Staff Attorney, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
On March 27, 2020, President Trump signed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) into law.[1]
The law provided aid to the U.S. economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. The CARES Act authorized the Small Business Administration (SBA) to create a loan guarantee program, the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), in response to the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on small businesses. The PPP helped participating businesses meet payroll needs and utilities, including employee salaries, sick leave, other paid leave, and health insurance expenses. Provided that credit union lenders complied with the applicable lender obligations set forth in the SBA's interim final rule (IFR), the SBA fully guaranteed loans issued under the PPP. Most federally insured credit unions (FICUs) were eligible to make PPP loans to members.[2]
Under the CARES Act, PPP loans received a zero percent risk weighting under the NCUA's risk-based capital requirements.[3]
On April 27, 2020, the Board issued an IFR (April 27th IFR) to make a conforming amendment to its capital adequacy regulation following the enactment of the CARES Act.[4]
As noted, the CARES Act required that, under the NCUA's risk-based capital requirements, PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weighting. To reflect the statutory requirement, the April 27th IFR amended the NCUA's capital adequacy regulation to provide that covered PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weight. The April 27th IFR also provided that the covered loan could be excluded from a credit union's accounting of total assets in its net worth ratio calculation if the covered loan was pledged as collateral for a non-recourse loan that was provided as part of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System's (FRB) PPP Loan Facility. The April 27th IFR also made a conforming amendment to the definition of commercial loan in the NCUA's member business loans and commercial lending rule. The Board found good cause to issue the April 27th IFR without advance notice-and-comment procedures and with an effective date upon publication.
This rule adopts as final the revisions to the capital adequacy rule and the member business lending rule published in the
Federal Register
on April 27, 2020.[5]
The Board is adopting this IFR as final. Under this final rule, FICUs may continue to assign a zero percent risk weight to PPP loans under the NCUA's risk-based capital regulations and neutralize the regulatory capital effects of participating in the PPP Liquidity Facility (PPP Loan Facility). Because the IFR was effective immediately upon publication and the final rule does not require affected parties to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect, the Board is issuing this final rule to address the types of matters described in this paragraph with an immediate effective date.[6]
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this final rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act and its specific rulemaking authority under the various provisions the Board administers.[7]
II. Final Rule
A. Zero Percent Risk Weight for PPP Loans
The NCUA's April 27th IFR amended the NCUA's risk-based net worth rules to reflect the requirement that PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weight. In particular, the IFR classified PPP loans as low-risk assets. Under prior § 702.106(d), low-risk assets received a zero percent risk weight.[8]
In addition, § 702.104(d) defined low-risk assets as cash on hand (for example, coin and currency, including vault, ATM and teller cash), the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund deposit, debt instruments unconditionally guaranteed by the NCUA, and loans issued under the SBA's PPP.[9]
Thus, the April 27th IFR provided that PPP loans received a zero percent risk weight under the NCUA's risk-based capital rules as required by the CARES Act.
The NCUA's 2015 final rule regarding risk-based capital (2015 Final Rule) [10]
went into effect on January 1, 2022,[11]
making substantial changes to the NCUA's previous prompt corrective action (PCA) requirements under part 702 of the NCUA's regulations. Among other changes, the 2015 Final Rule eliminated the definition of “low risk asset” under § 702.104(d). To account for this change, in a December 23, 2021, final rule on capital adequacy (December 2021 Final Rule), the NCUA gave covered loans issued under the SBA's PPP a zero percent risk weight.[12]
This amendment finalized the change made to the previous PCA regulations by the April 27th IFR, thus this final rule does not affect the changes that were made by the NCUA's December 2021 Final Rule and no further amendment is required.
B. Definition of Total Assets for Purposes of Calculating the Net Worth Ratio
Pursuant to section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, the FRB authorized each of the Federal Reserve Banks to participate in the PPP Loan Facility as a means to provide liquidity to small business lenders and the broader credit markets, help stabilize the financial system, and provide economic relief to
( printed page 69494)
small businesses nationwide.[13]
Through the PPP Loan Facility, each of the Federal Reserve Banks extended non-recourse loans to eligible financial institutions to fund PPP loans. Under this construct, only PPP loans that were guaranteed by the SBA with respect to both principal and interest and were originated by an eligible institution could be pledged as collateral to the Federal Reserve Banks. Participation in the PPP Loan Facility affected a FICU's balance sheet because, as a function of participating in the PPP Loan Facility, the FICU was required to originate and hold PPP covered loans (that is, assets that are eligible collateral pledged to the Federal Reserve Banks) on its balance sheet.
As a result, FICUs that participated in the PPP Loan Facility could potentially be subject to increased regulatory capital requirements due to the increase in total assets from originating and holding PPP loans. To facilitate use of the PPP Loan Facility, the April 27th IFR allowed FICUs to neutralize the regulatory capital effects of PPP loans pledged to the PPP Loan Facility.[14]

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
On February 25, 2026, NCUA (or `agency') published a proposed rule to solicit comments on the removal of a provision of NCUA regulations regarding federal credit unions' (FCUs) statutory lien authority. Upon further consideration, and based on the comments received, the Board is issuing this final rule, as proposed, to remove the term, “except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law.” This language does not provide any assistance to FCUs in determining whether such statutory or case law exists, therefore it has no material value.
DATES:
This final rule is effective December 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Gira Bose, Senior Staff Attorney,
Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6562 or
gbose@ncua.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
Section 701.39 of the NCUA's regulations implements the statutory lien authority granted to FCUs under the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act).[1]
The regulation, which converted a prior policy statement into a regulation in 1999, states that an FCU has the power to impress and enforce a lien against a member's shares and dividends to satisfy any outstanding financial obligation owed to the credit union.[2]
The proposed rule, issued on February 25, 2026, put forward an amendment to the regulation by removing the definition of the term “[e]xcept as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law.” [3]
The Board determined that this definition is not helpful. The fact that an FCU must determine which laws apply to its operations and must be aware that some legal requirements supersede others, is a universal consideration and not one that is specific to this regulation. Thus, the Board proposed to repeal paragraph 701.39(a)(1).
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).[4]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.[5]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.[6]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.[7]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on April 27, 2026, the Board had received 11 comments. Commenters were two credit unions, five state and regional credit union leagues or associations, three national credit union trade associations, and one individual member of the public who did not disclose a group affiliation. After careful consideration of the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments. Nine of the eleven commenters expressed support for the proposal generally stating that:
the provision identified for removal is redundant and does not provide substantive guidance to credit unions;
the proposal would remove potentially confusing language from NCUA's regulation and have no effect on lien authority or obligations; and
from an operational perspective, FCUs must already maintain processes to identify and apply applicable statutory and case law when exercising their authorities, including statutory lien rights. The presence or absence of this definitional language does not alter that responsibility.
Two commenters opposed the rule. One stated that preserving the current statutory lien framework best balances member transparency, operational certainty, and safety and soundness. The other commenter did not speak specifically to this proposal, but voiced opposition to deregulation in general. This commenter stated that the suggestion that certain requirements are overly burdensome warrants careful scrutiny. A regulation requiring staff time or administrative effort does not necessarily indicate that the requirement lacks value. Oversight, documentation, and verification processes inevitably require time and resources, but those efforts are part of maintaining responsible governance and protecting member assets.
The Board agrees that deregulatory proposals must be carefully considered and appropriately balanced with the need to maintain the safety and soundness of the credit union system. The Board also believes that this amendment will not jeopardize that balance. As a number of commenters noted, the term “except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law” does not provide any assistance to FCUs in determining whether such statutory or
( printed page 69492)
case law exists. And its removal does not diminish an FCU's obligation to determine, as in all cases, if there are other laws that apply to its activities. Thus, this rule is being finalized as proposed.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to Executive Order 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order. Executive Order 13563 (“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in Executive Order 12866. This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with Executive Order 12866 and Executive Order 13563. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined in section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
The Controlled Substances Act (CSA) grants the Attorney General authority to promulgate and enforce rules and regulations pertaining to the registration and control of the manufacture, distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances and the maintenance and submission of records and reports related thereto.[1]
The CSA further authorizes the Attorney General to promulgate regulations necessary and appropriate to execute the functions of subchapter I (Control and Enforcement) and subchapter II (Import and Export) of the CSA.[2]
The Attorney General has delegated this authority to the Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).[3]
Technical Amendment
DEA regulations state that an application shall be deemed to be withdrawn if an applicant requests an application to be returned, or if an applicant fails to respond to official correspondence regarding the application when sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested.[4]
The use of the term “applicant” may inadvertently suggest that this provision applies only to new registration applications and is not applicable to registration renewal applications. In this final rule, DEA is adding “or registrant” after “applicant” in 21 CFR 1301.16(b) to clarify that this provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications.

Administrative Procedure Act
An agency may find good cause to exempt a rule from certain provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including those requiring the publication of a prior notice of proposed rulemaking and the opportunity for public comment, if such actions are determined to be unnecessary, impracticable, or contrary to the public interest.[5]
The “unnecessary” prong of the APA good cause provision covers amendments that are “ `minor or merely technical' and of little public interest,” [6]
or that involve “routine determination[s], insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry . . . and to the public.” [7]
This rule contains only a technical amendment: it merely resolves a potential ambiguity by clarifying that the DEA regulation [8]
regarding amendments to and withdrawal of applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications. DEA has always understood and applied the regulation at 21 CFR 1301.16(b) to include renewals. DEA has accordingly determined that notice and comment are not required.
Similarly, the APA provides that a delayed effective date is unnecessary when the agency finds good cause for dispensing with the delay. The APA's delayed-effective-date provision is intended “to give affected parties time to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.” [9]
Here, regulated parties will not need any time to adjust their behavior to the changes made in this final rule because the rule does no more than ensure that the regulatory text of 21 CFR 1301.16(b) more clearly indicates the way that DEA has always understood and applied that provision.
In addition, the APA excepts from the requirements of notice and comment and a delayed effective date those rules that are non-substantive.[10]
Substantive rules make “substantive changes in prior regulations” or “create new law, rights, or duties.” [11]
Here, as already explained, this final rule makes no substantive changes in DEA's regulations because this rule simply clarifies the way that 21 CFR 1301.16(b) has always been understood and applied.
Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192 (Regulatory Review)
DEA has determined that this rulemaking is not a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review). Accordingly, this final rule has not been submitted to the Office of Management and Budget for review. This final rule was developed in accordance with section 1(b) of E.O. 12866, section 1(b) of E.O. 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and E.O. 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation).
As stated above, this final rule is a technical amendment to clarify that the provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications also applies to applications for registration renewal. DEA has always applied this provision to both new and renewal applications, and therefore, this final rule does not impose any new or substantive requirements on the public or DEA registrants. AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
( printed page 69502)
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary special local regulation (SLR) for the navigable waters of the Atlantic Ocean surrounding the Key West Main Shipping Channel and the waters between Sunset Key and Wisteria Island. This action is necessary to provide for the safety of life on these navigable waters near Key West, FL during the Race World Offshore World Championship 2026 event beginning on November 4, 2026, and ending on November 8, 2026. This regulation prohibits persons and vessels from entering the regulated area unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port Key West or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 9:00 a.m. on November 4, 2026, through 6 p.m. on November 8, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact MSTC Mathew Mason, Sector Key West Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 305-292-8823, or email
Mathew.R.Mason@uscg.mil.

II. Background and Authority
On August 5, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that they will sponsor a high-speed powerboat race. The Coast Guard received a request under 33 CFR 100.15 from the Race World Offshore Organization for a Marine Event Permit to host a high-speed powerboat race within the Key West Main Shipping Channel. The event will be held from 9:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. on November 4, 6, and 8, 2026, in Key West, FL. The races will include approximately 80 participants and 300 spectator craft.
The Captain of the Port Key West (COTP) is issuing this special local regulation (SLR) under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70041. The COTP has determined that potential hazards associated with the operation of vessels at high speeds include the possibility of collision within the navigable channel, as well as the possibility that participants operating within approaches to local public and private boat facilities might collide with or otherwise interfere with boaters near those facilities. The purpose of this rulemaking is to protect event participants, spectators, and transiting vessels before, during, and after the scheduled event.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. The Coast Guard was notified of the final details of the event concerning spectator locations and confirming event boundaries until October 29, 2026, but we must establish this SLR by November 4, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reasons, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary SLR from 9:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. on November 4, 6, and 8, 2026. The special local regulation will cover all navigable waters within 800 feet of the Racecourse and the navigable waters extending outward 300 feet from the North shoreline of Sunset Key. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the regulated area without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.

A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, 5 U.S.C. 601-612, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.

Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under Executive Order 13132, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.

articles.full_text: The Department is effectuating nomenclature changes throughout Title 15 of the Code of Federal Regulations to remove all references to an outdated official title ("Assistant General Counsel for Employment, Litigation and Information") and replace them with updated references to the appropriate official (the "Assistant General Counsel for Litigation and Strategic Support" or the "Assistant General Counsel for Information Security and Emerging Technologies"). This action is necessary to reflect the current structure and roles within the Department and to ensure that the regulations at Title 15 remain up to date and refer the public to the appropriate officials. This action is intended to promote clarity and efficiency without making any substantive changes to any regulations.
